title: Thinking in pipelines
summary: See a query as items flowing through stages, and translate freely between loops, method syntax and query syntax.

steps.title: Items flow one at a time
body: In module 6 you learned that a query is a recipe. Here is the picture to keep in your head: a **pipeline**. Each operator is a stage, and items travel through the stages **one at a time**.

`5` does not wait for the whole array to be filtered. It passes `Where`, becomes `50` in `Select`, and reaches `Take` before `3` has even been looked at. When `Take` has three items it stops asking, so `9` and `4` are **never touched**.
Press play below and watch each number travel.

steps.prompt: Both lambdas print as they run. What does this print?
steps.explain: Each item goes all the way down the pipe before the next one starts. `1` fails `Where`, so it never reaches `Select`: you see `W1` with no `S1` after it.

steps.title: Query syntax, the full picture
body: Module 6 showed `from`, `where`, `orderby`, `select`. Query syntax has a few more clauses, and each one is just a method call in disguise:
| `let y = x * 2` | `.Select(x => new { x, y = x * 2 })` |
`let` is the one method syntax lacks. It names a value you computed so later clauses can reuse it:
var taxed = from o in orders
A query must end with `select` or `group`.

steps.prompt: Match each query clause to the method it turns into.
Which method chain does the same as this query?
options: `orders.Select(o => new { o, tax = o.Total * 0.2m }).Where(x => x.tax > 10).OrderBy(x => x.o.Customer).ThenByDescending(x => x.tax).Select(x => $"{x.o.Customer}: {x.tax}")`
`orders.Select(o => new { o, tax = o.Total * 0.2m }).Where(x => x.tax > 10).OrderBy(x => x.o.Customer).OrderByDescending(x => x.tax).Select(x => $"{x.o.Customer}: {x.tax}")`
steps.explain: `let` becomes a `Select` into an anonymous object that carries both the order and the new value. A second key in `orderby` is a `ThenBy`, never a second `OrderBy` (that would throw the first sort away).

steps.title: Every loop shape has an operator
body: Most loops you write are made of the same few moves. Each has a LINQ name:
is `temps.TakeWhile(t => t < 22).Select(t => t * 2).ToList()`. Watch `TakeWhile` stop the whole pipe at the first warm day.

steps.prompt: `TakeWhile`, `Where` and `SkipWhile` on the same temperatures. What does this print?
steps.explain: `TakeWhile` is a `break`: it stops for good at `25`, so the later `19` is lost. `Where` is a `continue`: it checks every item. `SkipWhile` drops items only until the first failure, then lets everything through, including `19`.

steps.prompt: Arrange the query: films rated over 8, scored out of 100, best score first, as titles.
lines: var picks = from m in movies
also: var picks = from m in movies
steps.explain: `from` opens the query and `select` closes it. `let` must come before anything that uses `score`. Filtering before sorting is the usual habit (less to sort), but both orders give the same result.

steps.title: Loop to LINQ: error messages
prompt: Log lines look like `ERROR Disk full` or `INFO Started`. This loop collects error messages. Rewrite the body as **one LINQ query with no loop**. It must behave exactly the same:
- the message is the text after `"ERROR "`, trimmed
- skip messages that are empty after trimming
template: var dojoLog = new List<string> { "INFO Started", "ERROR Disk full", "ERROR    ", "WARN Slow", "ERROR timeout ", "ERROR auth failed", "ERROR late one" };
Dojo.Eq("keeps the first three non-empty errors", new List<string> { "DISK FULL", "TIMEOUT", "AUTH FAILED" }, ErrorMessages(dojoLog));
Dojo.Eq("no errors gives an empty list", new List<string>(), ErrorMessages(new List<string> { "INFO a", "WARN b" }));
Dojo.Eq("a line starting with ERRORS is not an error", new List<string> { "X" }, ErrorMessages(new List<string> { "ERRORS x", "ERROR x" }));
hints: Each `continue` becomes a `Where`, each computed value a `Select`, the `break` a `Take`.
Order matters: trim in a `Select` before the `Where` that checks the length.

steps.title: LINQ to loop: word counts
prompt: Now the other way. This query counts words in a sentence. Rewrite it with a `foreach` loop and a `Dictionary`, **without** calling `Select`, `Where`, `GroupBy`, `ToDictionary` or `Count`.
`WordCounts("The cat and THE dog and the end")` has `the` â†’ 3, `and` â†’ 2, `cat`, `dog`, `end` â†’ 1.
template: var dojoC = WordCounts("The cat and THE dog and the end");
Dojo.Eq("short words are skipped", 0, WordCounts("a an to of").Keys.Count);
Dojo.Eq("extra spaces are ignored", 2, WordCounts("  hey   hey ").GetValueOrDefault("hey"));

forbid.message: Does not use Select, Where, GroupBy, ToDictionary or Count()

hints: `Select` becomes a line inside the loop, `Where` becomes `if (...) continue;`.
`GroupBy` + `Count` together are "add one to this word's counter".
`counts[w] = counts.GetValueOrDefault(w) + 1;` handles both a new word and a seen one.

steps.title: Query syntax: top picks
prompt: The tests define `record Movie(string Title, int Year, double Rating, string Genre);`
Write `static List<string> TopPicks(List<Movie> movies, string genre)` using **query syntax** (`from ... select`), not `.Where(...)`.
- only movies of that `genre` with a `Rating` of 8 or more
- highest rating first; equal ratings by `Title` A to Z
starter: static List<string> TopPicks(List<Movie> movies, string genre)
var picks = from m in movies
solution: static List<string> TopPicks(List<Movie> movies, string genre)
var picks = from m in movies
template: Dojo.Eq("Crime picks, ties by title", new List<string> { "Casino (1995)", "Heat (1995)", "Fargo (1996)" }, TopPicks(dojoMovies, "Crime"));
Dojo.Eq("unknown genre gives nothing", new List<string>(), TopPicks(dojoMovies, "Western"));
record Movie(string Title, int Year, double Rating, string Genre);

forbid.message: Does not call Where or OrderBy directly

hints: `orderby m.Rating descending, m.Title` sorts by rating then title.
